pos: v. (third person singular of load; heaps a burden upon)
etymology: Saxon hladan, to lade or heap on. In Psalm 68:19 it renders the Hebrew 'amas, to load or lade a beast.
biblical_def: Psalm 68 is the psalm of the ascending God, and its highest line uses the language of a pack animal: “Blessed be the Lord, who daily loadeth us with benefits, even the God of our salvation. Selah” (Psalm 68:19). The Hebrew verb is the one used of lading a donkey — piling a burden on until the beast is laden. The psalmist deliberately turns it. God loads His people, and what He loads them with is benefits, and He does it daily. The Authorized Version uses loadeth once. The next verse names what makes the loading possible: “He that is our God is the God of salvation; and unto GOD the Lord belong the issues from death” (Psalm 68:20). Paul quotes this psalm's eighteenth verse of Christ's ascension and giving of gifts, which sets the nineteenth verse where the Reformed tradition has always read it — the ascended Christ daily lading His church with the benefits He purchased. The dictionary notes the pastoral force. Mercies are not rationed out as the believer earns them; they are heaped on, every day, by a God who has already dealt with death. “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psalm 103:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): LOAD, verb transitive To lay on a burden; to put on or in something to be carried; to lade.
webster_full: LOAD, verb transitive To lay on a burden; to put on or in something to be carried, or something oppressive.
2. To encumber; to lay on or in something heavy.
3. To charge, as a gun.
4. To make heavy by something added or appended.
LOAD, noun A burden; that which is laid on or put in any thing for conveyance.
scriptures: Blessed be the Lord, who daily loadeth us with benefits, even the God of our salvation. Selah.
He that is our God is the God of salvation; and unto GOD the Lord belong the issues from death.
Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:
corruption_summary: Daily mercies are now described as abundance or flow; Scripture says God lades His people like a beast of burden, with benefits.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern spirituality of abundance speaks of flow, alignment, and receiving — language that leaves out the Giver and the ground of the giving. Psalm 68:19 names both: it is the Lord who loads, and He is the God of our salvation, and verse 20 says the issues from death belong to Him. Benefits detached from the God of salvation are not the psalm's subject.

The principle to recover is the daily measure. Not occasionally, not in proportion to our faithfulness, but daily loadeth. Psalm 103:2 shows the corresponding duty: the only thing a believer is told to do with so many benefits is to bless the LORD and not forget them.

roots_lines: Saxon hladan, to lade, heap on, burden.
Hebrew 'amas, to load or lade, used of pack animals.

pos: adj. (comparative of fat; better fed, fuller in flesh)
etymology: Saxon faet, fat, with the comparative ending. In Daniel 1:15 it renders a Hebrew word for fatness or plumpness of flesh.
biblical_def: Daniel and his three companions refuse the king's table and ask for pulse and water for ten days. The result is reported plainly: “And at the end of ten days their countenances appeared fairer and fatter in flesh than all the children which did eat the portion of the king's meat” (Daniel 1:15). The Authorized Version uses fatter once. The dictionary is careful about what this verse does and does not establish. It does not establish a diet. The point of the chapter is stated in verse 8: “But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat” (Daniel 1:8). This was a conscience matter about defilement — meat from a pagan table, offered to idols, unclean by the law — and the vegetables were the only safe option available, not a health programme. God vindicated the conscience, and then gave something better than looks: “As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom” (Daniel 1:17). Four captive boys kept the law of their God in the king's own house, and God made them the wisest men in Babylon.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FAT, adjective Fleshy; plump; corpulent; abounding with fat. Comparative, fatter.
webster_full: FAT, adjective Fleshy; plump; corpulent; abounding with an oily concrete substance.
2. Coarse; gross.
3. Dull; heavy; stupid; unteachable.
4. Rich; wealthy; affluent.
FATNESS, noun The quality of being fat; also, fertility; richness; that which gives fertility.
scriptures: Dan 1:15
And at the end of ten days their countenances appeared fairer and fatter in flesh than all the children which did eat the portion of the king's meat.
Dan 1:8

But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.
Dan 1:17
As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.
corruption_summary: Daniel 1 is marketed as a diet plan; the chapter is about conscience, defilement, and God's vindication of obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: The commercial misuse of this chapter is well known: a named eating programme sold on the authority of a verse about captive Hebrew boys refusing idol-meat. Daniel 1:8 states the issue — defilement — and the pulse was what was left once the defiled food was declined. To read it as nutritional advice is to miss the whole chapter.

The principle to recover is that God honours conscience bound by His word. The faces were an outward sign; the real gift was knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom, and understanding in visions and dreams. Daniel kept the law of his God in Babylon and outlasted the empire that captured him.

roots_lines: Saxon faet, fat; the comparative ending -ter.
Hebrew bari', fat, plump, well-fed.
Daniel 1:15 is the only place the Authorized Version uses fatter.
Daniel's refusal was about defilement, not about nutrition.
The greater gift followed in verse 17: knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom.

pos: adj. (comparative of fresh; newer, more vigorous)
etymology: Saxon fersc, fresh, new, with the comparative ending. In Job 33:25 it renders a Hebrew word for tenderness or freshness of flesh.
biblical_def: Elihu describes God's dealing with a man brought to the edge of the pit and then recovered: “His flesh shall be fresher than a child's: he shall return to the days of his youth” (Job 33:25). The Authorized Version uses fresher once. It stands in the middle of the most gospel-shaped speech in the book, because the verse before it is this: “Then he is gracious unto him, and saith, Deliver him from going down to the pit: I have found a ransom” (Job 33:24). A ransom found, the pit refused, the flesh made fresher than a child's, and then prayer and a seen face and rendered righteousness (Job 33:26). The dictionary reads this as a true word spoken by a flawed speaker. Elihu is not rebuked at the end of the book as the three friends are, and what he says here about a ransom points beyond any chastening-and-recovery to the only ransom that delivers from the pit. The freshness promised is bodily — a man restored from sickness — and in the resurrection it is more than bodily. The flesh of the redeemed will be fresher than a child's, and the ransom that secures it was found by God, not by the man.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FRESH, adjective New; recently grown or made; not stale; also, vigorous; healthy. Comparative, fresher.
webster_full: FRESH, adjective Moving with celerity; brisk; strong; vigorous.
2. Having the colour and appearance of young thrifty plants; lively; not impaired or faded.
3. New; recently grown; as fresh vegetables.
4. Not salt; as fresh water.
FRESHNESS, noun Newness; vigour; spirit; the contrary of vapidness.
scriptures: His flesh shall be fresher than a child's: he shall return to the days of his youth:
Then he is gracious unto him, and saith, Deliver him from going down to the pit: I have found a ransom.
He shall pray unto God, and he will be favourable unto him: and he shall see his face with joy: for he will render unto man his righteousness.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The misuse worth naming is the healing-ministry one, which reads Job 33:25 as a blanket promise of physical restoration claimable at will. Elihu is describing God's ordinary dealing with a chastened man, not issuing a guarantee; Job himself was restored, but Paul was left with a thorn and Trophimus was left sick at Miletum.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ransom of verse 24. It is God who says, I have found a ransom — the finding is His, not the sufferer's — and the freshness of the flesh follows from it. That order is the gospel's order.

roots_lines: Saxon fersc, fresh, new, unimpaired.
Hebrew rutaphash, to be fresh or tender in flesh.
Job 33:25 is the only place the Authorized Version uses fresher.

pos: adj. (comparative of soft; smoother, more yielding to the touch)
etymology: Saxon softe, soft, gentle, with the comparative ending. In Psalm 55:21 it renders a Hebrew word for smoothness or oiliness of speech.
biblical_def: David writes of a betrayal by a familiar friend, and his description of the man is a masterpiece of two-part sentences: “The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords” (Psalm 55:21). Smoother than butter — war in the heart. Softer than oil — drawn swords. The Authorized Version uses softer once. The grief of the psalm is not the enmity but its source: “For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it” (Psalm 55:12). An enemy's hatred can be carried. A counsellor's oiled words cannot. The dictionary reads this psalm with the Ahithophel narrative in view, and beyond it with the greater betrayal — a kiss in a garden, the softest thing a man can do with his mouth, used as the sign to the officers. And the psalm supplies the only answer there is: “Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved” (Psalm 55:22). Soft speech is not evidence of a soft heart, and Scripture nowhere invites us to judge a man by how pleasant he is to hear.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SOFT, adjective Easily yielding to pressure; also, mild; gentle; smooth; flattering. Comparative, softer.
webster_full: SOFT, adjective Easily yielding to pressure; the contrary of hard.
2. Not rough, rugged or harsh; smooth to the touch.
3. Mild; gentle; kind; not severe or unfeeling.
4. Mild; gentle; not loud or rough; as a soft voice.
5. Smooth; flattering; as soft words.
scriptures: The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.
For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it: neither was it he that hated me that did magnify himself against me; then I would have hid myself from him:
Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.
corruption_summary: Gentleness of manner is widely treated as proof of a right heart; Psalm 55:21 says the softest words can be drawn swords.
corruption_paragraphs: The contemporary standard for judging a teacher or a counsellor is very largely tone. A man who speaks warmly, inclusively, and without sharp edges is assumed to be safe, and a man who speaks plainly is assumed to be harsh. Psalm 55:21 destroys that test: the words were softer than oil and they were drawn swords, and the man who spoke them had war in his heart.

The principle to recover is that content, not texture, is the test. Scripture commends gentleness genuinely — a soft answer turneth away wrath — and it warns in the same breath that flattery is a net. Psalm 55:22 directs the betrayed believer not to a strategy but to the LORD, who sustains and will never suffer the righteous to be moved.

etymology: Icelandic skil, distinction, discernment, through skilful, with the ending -ly. In Psalm 33:3 it renders a Hebrew word meaning to do well or to do a thing beautifully.
biblical_def: The command to sing in Psalm 33 comes with a command about how: “Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise” (Psalm 33:3). The Authorized Version uses skilfully once, and it is in a worship rubric. Three verses govern the opening of the psalm: rejoice, for praise is comely for the upright (Psalm 33:1); praise with harp and the psaltery and an instrument of ten strings (Psalm 33:2); sing a new song and play skilfully and loudly (Psalm 33:3). Skill is commanded, and so is volume. The dictionary notes both halves without flattening either. God is not honoured by carelessness; the Levitical musicians were trained men, and the Hebrew behind skilfully means to do a thing well and beautifully. At the same time skill is commanded as a servant of praise, never as a performance for men — the object throughout is unto him. The dictionary holds the regulative principle of worship, and reads these instruments as belonging to the ordered worship of the old covenant temple; what carries forward unchanged is the standard. Whatever God has appointed His people to do in worship, He has appointed them to do well.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SKILFULLY, adverb With skill; with nice art; dextrously; with readiness in performance.
webster_full: SKILFULLY, adverb With skill; with nice art; dextrously.
SKILFUL, adjective Knowing; well versed in any art; hence, dextrous; able in management.
2. Well versed in practice; expert.
SKILFULNESS, noun The quality of possessing skill; dextrousness; ability to perform well.
SKILL, noun The familiar knowledge of any art or science, united with readiness and dexterity in execution.
scriptures: Psa 33:3
Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise.
Psa 33:1
Rejoice in the LORD, O ye righteous: for praise is comely for the upright.
Psa 33:2
Praise the LORD with harp: sing unto him with the psaltery and an instrument of ten strings.
corruption_summary: Skill in worship is now pursued as production value; the psalm commands it as service rendered unto Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern worship industry has taken the command to play skilfully and detached it from the object. Excellence is pursued for the sake of the experience, the atmosphere, and the audience, and the result is performance with a congregation watching. The psalm fixes the direction three times: unto him a new song, unto him with the psaltery, praise the LORD with harp.

The principle to recover is the opposite error's cure as well. Carelessness is not humility. Praise is comely for the upright, skill is commanded, and the sound is to be loud. God does not ask His people to do badly what He has told them to do.

roots_lines: Icelandic skil, distinction or discernment; English skill.

etymology: Saxon spedan, to succeed or prosper. The older English sense of speed is success, not haste. In Judges 5:30 it renders a Hebrew verb for finding or obtaining.
biblical_def: The song of Deborah ends with one of the cruellest scenes in Scripture, and it is imagined rather than reported. Sisera's mother is at the window watching for a chariot that will never come (Judges 5:28), and her wise ladies answer her with the only explanation they can bear: “Have they not sped? have they not divided the prey; to every man a damsel or two; to Sisera a prey of divers colours” (Judges 5:30). Sped here means prospered, succeeded — the older English sense, from which our word speed descends. The women assume the delay is because the plunder is being counted. And the plunder they name first is women: to every man a damsel or two. The Authorized Version uses sped once. The dictionary notes that the song does not soften the mothers of Israel's enemies into innocents; it shows a household entirely comfortable with the rape of captured girls, waiting for its share. And then the song closes: “So let all thine enemies perish, O LORD: but let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might” (Judges 5:31). Sisera had not sped. Jael had.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SPED, preterit tense and participle passive of speed. Prospered; succeeded; dispatched.
webster_full: SPED, preterit tense and participle passive of speed.
SPEED, verb intransitive To make haste; to move with celerity.
2. To have success; to prosper; to succeed; to be fortunate.
SPEED, noun Swiftness; quickness; celerity; haste.
2. Success; prosperity in an undertaking; as, to wish one good speed.
scriptures: Jdg 5:30
Have they not sped? have they not divided the prey; to every man a damsel or two; to Sisera a prey of divers colours
Jdg 5:28
The mother of Sisera looked out at a window, and cried through the lattice, Why is his chariot so long in coming? why tarry the wheels of his chariots?
Jdg 5:31
So let all thine enemies perish, O LORD: but let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might. And the land had rest forty years.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: Two readings go wrong. One treats Judges 5:28-30 as a note of pity inviting sympathy for Sisera's mother against Israel's triumph; the verse she speaks is about dividing captured girls, and the song gives her no such sympathy. The other dismisses the whole chapter as tribal savagery, which refuses to read it as the inspired Scripture it is.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the closing prayer of verse 31. Deborah does not gloat over a woman at a lattice; she asks that all the LORD's enemies perish and all who love Him shine like the sun, and the chapter ends with forty years of rest for a people who had been oppressed twenty.

pos: v. (participle of ride; borne upon, as upon a beast)
etymology: Saxon ridan, to ride. In Numbers 22:30 it renders the Hebrew rakab, to ride or mount.
biblical_def: The LORD opens the mouth of Balaam's ass, and the first thing she says is a reproach and the second is an argument from long service: “And the ass said unto Balaam, Am not I thine ass, upon which thou hast ridden ever since I was thine unto this day? was I ever wont to do so unto thee? And he said, Nay” (Numbers 22:30). The Authorized Version uses ridden once. The dictionary notes the astonishing economy of the scene. A prophet-for-hire is beating a beast that has just saved his life three times; the beast reasons with him better than he has reasoned with God; and Balaam, who has been talking with the Almighty for two chapters, is not even surprised to be answered by a donkey. Only then are his eyes opened: “Then the LORD opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the way, and his sword drawn in his hand” (Numbers 22:31). The animal saw the drawn sword from the start. Peter calls this the madness of the prophet rebuked by a dumb ass, and the dictionary reads it as Scripture's own comment on covetous prophecy: a man who has priced his gift sees less than his mount.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): RIDDEN, participle passive of ride. Borne; carried, as on horseback.
webster_full: RIDDEN, participle passive of ride.

2. To be borne on or in a fluid; to float.
3. To be supported in motion.

And the LORD opened the mouth of the ass, and she said unto Balaam, What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times?

corruption_summary: The speaking ass is widely treated as folklore; Scripture reports it as history and the apostle Peter cites it as fact.
corruption_paragraphs: The critical handling of Numbers 22 classifies the speaking ass as legendary material or folk motif embedded in the Pentateuch. The dictionary rejects that framing. Moses wrote the book, the event is reported as event, and 2 Peter 2:16 refers to it as a real rebuke of a real prophet by a dumb ass speaking with man's voice.

The principle to recover is what the miracle exposes. The beast saw the angel; the prophet did not. A man whose gift is for sale loses discernment first, and God can open a donkey's mouth as readily as a prophet's.

pos: v. (past of outlive; lived longer than another)
etymology: English out and live. The Authorized Version's margin reads prolonged days after Joshua, which is the Hebrew idiom.
biblical_def: The book of Judges gives the hinge of Israel's whole decline in three verses, and the first turns on this word: “And the people served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders that outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great works of the LORD, that he did for Israel” (Judges 2:7). Obedience lasted exactly as long as living memory. The elders who had seen the works kept the people straight; when they died, so did the faithfulness: “And also all that generation were gathered unto their fathers: and there arose another generation after them, which knew not the LORD, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel” (Judges 2:10). And then: “And the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD, and served Baalim” (Judges 2:11). The Authorized Version uses outlived once. The dictionary reads this as the most practical warning in the Old Testament about catechism. A generation that knew the works of God was not able to transmit them merely by having witnessed them. Deuteronomy had commanded teaching diligently unto the children, and Judges 2 is the record of what happens where that command is dropped: one funeral and the nation turns.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): OUTLIVE, verb transitive To live beyond; to survive; to live longer than another.
webster_full: OUTLIVE, verb transitive To live beyond; to survive.
OUTLIVED, participle passive Survived.
OUTLIVER, noun One who lives longer than another; a survivor.

SURVIVE, verb transitive To outlive; to live beyond the life of another.
scriptures: Jdg 2:7
And the people served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders that outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great works of the LORD, that he did for Israel.
Jdg 2:10

Jdg 2:11
And the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD, and served Baalim:
corruption_summary: Faith is widely assumed to pass down by osmosis; Judges 2 records a nation apostatising within one generation of eyewitnesses.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern household assumption is that children raised near Christianity will absorb it. Judges 2 is the refutation. The elders had seen the Jordan opened and Jericho fall; their children knew neither the LORD nor the works, and the next sentence is that Israel served Baalim. Proximity to a believing generation taught nobody anything.

The principle to recover is deliberate instruction. Deuteronomy 6 commands teaching diligently unto the children, talking of the commandments in the house and by the way and at lying down and rising up. Family worship and catechism are not optional enrichments; Judges 2:10 is what their absence produces, and it takes exactly one funeral.

pos: v. (third person singular of owe; is indebted)
etymology: Saxon agan, to own or possess, hence to be bound to render. In Philemon 1:18 it renders the Greek opheilei, from opheilo, to owe.
biblical_def: Paul sends a runaway slave back to his master with the shortest and clearest statement of imputation in the New Testament outside Romans: “If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account” (Philemon 1:18). The Authorized Version uses oweth once. Onesimus had run and, it seems, taken something with him; Paul does not minimise the debt, dispute it, or ask Philemon to waive it. He transfers it. The next verse makes it legally binding and signs it: “I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it” (Philemon 1:19). A debt really owed by one man, charged to the account of another who did not incur it, discharged by the second man's own promise — that is the structure of justification, and the apostle enacts it in a private letter about a slave. The dictionary notes what Paul does not do. He does not say the wrong did not happen. Reconciliation in Scripture never proceeds by denying the debt; it proceeds by someone else paying it. He asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul, which is precisely how the Father receives the believer who comes in Christ's name.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): OWE, verb transitive To be indebted; to be obliged or bound to pay.
webster_full: OWE, verb transitive To be indebted; to be obliged or bound to pay.
2. To be obliged to ascribe to; to be obliged for; as, he owes his wealth to industry.
3. To possess; to have; to be the owner of. Obsolete.
OWETH, verb Third person singular of owe.
OWING, participle passive Due; that moral obligation requires to be paid.
scriptures: Phm 1:18
If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account;
Phm 1:19
I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it: albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides.
Phm 1:10
I beseech thee for my son Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my bonds:
corruption_summary: Philemon is read as either an endorsement of slavery or an early abolition tract; its doctrinal centre is substitution and imputed debt.
corruption_paragraphs: Two readings miss the letter. One cites it to show the apostle untroubled by slavery; another makes it a social manifesto. Paul does something more radical than either: he sends the slave back as a brother, tells the master to receive him as he would receive Paul, and puts the man's debt on his own account. The institution is undermined at the root by making the two men brethren, and Paul elsewhere commands masters to render what is just.

The principle to recover is the mechanism of verse 18. The debt is acknowledged, not denied; it is transferred, not waived; and it is discharged by the surety's own signature. That is imputation, and the whole of justification by faith is in those two verses.

etymology: Saxon oft, frequently, with the comparative ending. In Acts 24:26 it renders the Greek puknoteron, more frequently.
biblical_def: Felix has heard Paul reason of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, and has trembled and sent him away (Acts 24:25). Then Luke tells us why the governor kept calling him back: “He hoped also that money should have been given him of Paul, that he might loose him: wherefore he sent for him the oftener, and communed with him” (Acts 24:26). The Authorized Version uses oftener once, and it is one of the saddest words in Acts. Felix had more private access to apostolic preaching than almost anyone in the New Testament, and he sought it to negotiate a bribe. Two years of conversations, and the outcome is recorded in the next verse: “But after two years Porcius Festus came into Felix' room: and Felix, willing to shew the Jews a pleasure, left Paul bound” (Acts 24:27). The dictionary notes the doctrine plainly. Frequency of hearing is not the same as faith. A man may tremble under the word, come back for more of it, and be lost — and the convenient season Felix promised himself never came. Covetousness is what kept bringing him to the sermon and what kept him from the Christ it preached.

scriptures: He hoped also that money should have been given him of Paul, that he might loose him: wherefore he sent for him the oftener, and communed with him.
And as he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled, and answered, Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee.
But after two years Porcius Festus came into Felix' room: and Felix, willing to shew the Jews a pleasure, left Paul bound.
corruption_summary: Religious interest is widely mistaken for conversion; Felix trembled, listened often for two years, and perished bound to his bribe.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern measure of a man's spiritual state is engagement: he attends, he asks questions, he is moved. Felix met every one of those marks. He trembled under the preaching of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, and he sent for Paul the oftener — and his motive was money. Interest in the word is not the same thing as submission to it.

The principle to recover is the deceit of the convenient season. Felix had two years of convenient seasons and used them for negotiation. Scripture's word on that is now: today, if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.
